pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2). Using addition to find the total in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and writing an equation expressing the total as a sum of EQUAL ADDENDS — the array-to-repeated-addition bridge.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'solve problems … using … arrays, repeated addition …'; recorded with × signs as tables develop (Y2–Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends'.
• Operational details: read the array by ROWS — each row is an equal addend — and write 4+4+4 (three rows of four), then connect to 3×4. Emphasise the addends are EQUAL (that's what makes it a multiplication situation). This formalises the array as the pivot between addition and multiplication.
• Checkpoint: array → equal-addend equation. Tier A (7): count an array's total by adding rows. Tier B (7–8): write the equal-addend equation (4+4+4=12) for a 3-row array. Tier C (8): write both the addition and the multiplication for an array and explain the addends must be equal.
bestPractices: Read the array row by row so each row becomes one equal addend, then write the repeated-addition equation — making 'sum of equal addends' concrete before the × symbol.
Stress that the addends must be EQUAL: contrast an array (equal rows) with a ragged arrangement (unequal rows) that is NOT a multiplication situation.
Bridge to the × symbol by pairing the equal-addend equation with the multiplication (4+4+4 alongside 3×4), so children see multiplication as the shorthand.
Read the same array by columns too, foreshadowing commutativity (three 4s or four 3s).
Keep arrays within 5×5 and physically buildable, so the structure (rows/columns) is clear and countable.
keyRepresentations: Rectangular array read row-by-row (each row = one equal addend)
commonMisconceptions: Adding UNEQUAL groups and still writing it as a single multiplication (missing the equal-addends requirement).
Counting every object individually rather than adding equal rows.
Confusing the number of rows with the number in each row when writing the equation.
Not connecting the repeated-addition equation to the multiplication (seeing them as separate).
Miscounting by losing track of which rows have been added (no systematic row-by-row approach).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2): use addition to find the total of objects in a rectangular array (up to 5×5) and write an equation expressing the total as a sum of EQUAL addends, then bridge to the multiplication fact. The core insight is that each row of the array contributes one equal addend, so reading an array row by row turns it into repeated addition (4+4+4=12) and then into 3×4. Equality of the rows is what makes it a multiplication situation, so a ragged (unequal-row) arrangement serves as the key non-example.

activities.title: Sum the rows: build the equal-addend equation from an array
feedback: If the child writes 3+4 (rows plus row-size): shade one row to show it holds 4, then show that same 4 repeats for every row → 4+4+4. Name clearly that 'number of rows' and 'amount in each row' are two different things; the equation adds the row-amount once per row.

If the child gives the correct sum but justifies it only as 'because it makes 12': cover the rows one at a time so each shows the same 4, and name that the rows being equal is exactly what lets you add 4 repeatedly instead of counting every dot.

If the child insists on counting every dot and distrusts the shortcut: do NOT force the shortcut. Let them verify by counting a few arrays so repeated addition earns their trust over several examples.

For the ragged arrangement: confirm that because the rows are not equal you cannot write one repeated-equal-addend equation, so it is not a multiplication situation — this is the point of the contrast.
activities.rationale: Assembling 4+4+4 row by row makes 'sum of equal addends' concrete before the × symbol, and pairing it with 3×4 presents multiplication as shorthand for adding equal rows. Reading by columns previews commutativity (three 4s vs four 3s), and the ragged non-example isolates the equal-addends requirement that defines a multiplication situation.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems using arrays and repeated addition, recorded with multiplication signs as tables develop.
2.OA.4 use addition to find the total in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and write an equation expressing the total as a sum of equal addends.
learnerActions: Look at a 3×4 array (3 rows, 4 dots in each row) and point to one row to establish that it holds 4 dots.
Add the array one row at a time, saying and writing the running total: 4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4 = 12 — one addend per row.
After writing 4+4+4=12, write the matching multiplication 3×4=12 and say which number tells how many rows and which tells how many are in each row.
Read the same array by columns instead and write it as 3+3+3+3 (four 3s), noticing you get 12 again.
Now try a ragged arrangement where one row has 4 and another has 5; attempt to write a single equal-addend equation and explain why it will not form.
activities.intendedInsight: Each equal row of an array is one equal addend, so adding the rows gives the total; the multiplication fact is just the shorthand for adding equal rows, and this only works when the rows are equal.

activities.title: Draw an array for a given equation
feedback: If the number of rows and the amount per row get swapped, have the child count the addends in the equation (how many 5s? four) and match that to the number of rows drawn.
If rows are drawn unequal, point out that the equation uses the same number each time, so every row must hold the same amount.
activities.rationale: Constructing an array from a given equation requires producing structure rather than recognising it, strengthening the array↔equation bridge in both directions.
learnerActions: Given the equation 5+5+5+5, draw a rectangular array that matches it (four rows of five, or equivalently five columns of four).
Say aloud which part of the equation is the number of rows and which is the amount in each row.
Write the multiplication fact for your array (4×5 or 5×4) and check the total matches 20.
Explain why your drawing shows equal rows and how that connects back to the repeated addition.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can move in both directions — from array to equation and from equation to array — which shows they understand the equal-groups structure rather than just reading one off the other.

activities.title: Match and complete: array ↔ equal-addend equation ↔ multiplication
feedback: If a learner picks the unequal-addend distractor, draw the arrangement that equation would represent and shade its rows to show they are not equal, so it does not match the equal-rows array and cannot be written as one repeated-equal-addend equation.
If the addition and multiplication are seen as unrelated, place 4+4+4 beside 3×4 and count: three rows, four in each — the multiplication summarises the addition.
activities.rationale: Fill-in and matching tasks check the bridge crisply and surface whether a child still confuses adding equal rows with adding unequal groups. These are checks of recognition and completion; they confirm understanding but do not by themselves require independent construction, so pair them with the drawing and build-the-equation activities.
learnerActions: For a shown array, fill in the blanks of the equal-addend equation (__ + __ + __ = __).
Write the matching multiplication fact for the same array.

From a set of candidate equations, choose the one that matches a given equal-rows array; include a distractor that uses unequal addends (e.g., 3+4+5), which would correspond to a ragged arrangement and does not match.
Explain why the unequal-addend distractor cannot represent the equal-rows array as a single equal-addend equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and completing the correct equal-addend equation (and rejecting an unequal-addend distractor) confirms the array-to-repeated-addition bridge and the equal-addends requirement.

constraints: Keep arrays within 5×5 and physically buildable (counters, dots, or drawn grids) so rows and columns stay clear and countable.
Emphasise throughout that the addends must be EQUAL; always contrast the array with a ragged, unequal-row arrangement that is NOT a multiplication situation.

Matching/fill-in tasks assess recognition and completion; they do not on their own elicit independent construction of an array or equation, so include at least one task where the child builds an array from an equation or assembles the equation from scratch.

A static labelled array (tap- or lift-to-reveal addends and the × fact) is a useful reference and shows the bridge, but does not let the child build the sum row by row or test the equal-addends requirement dynamically; treat it as a scaffold, not a replacement for building.
Do not push the repeated-addition shortcut on a child who still needs to count every object to trust it; let repeated addition earn trust through several verified examples.

If optional on-screen interaction is used (tapping a row to drop its value into a running equation, a 'fold'/combine action collapsing 4+4+4 into 3×4, a rotate control to read by columns, a ragged-array mode), these are illustrative mechanisms to make the bridge visible, not required tooling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (CCSS-M 2.OA.4) is marked verified:false in the row; the exact-claim citations are carried over as-is and their verification status is unchanged.

Activity 2 (equation→array drawing) corresponds to the row's evidence item 'Draw a rectangular array to model a given repeated-addition equation', but no cited source claim directly supports the reverse-construction principle, so its sourceClaims is [] (topic-aligned, not evidence the reverse task is required).

Planar vs 3D: the original row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that dialogue 'adds little unique value'. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the sources; they have been dropped as universal laws. Arrays are naturally planar, so a flat representation fits the content, but no claim is made that other media cannot teach it.

Arithmetic self-check performed: 4+4+4=12 and 3×4=12 are correct; reading the same 3×4 array by columns gives 3+3+3+3=12 (four 3s), consistent with the commutativity preview. The 5+5+5+5 drawing example corresponds to 4×5=20. The Activity 3 distractor 3+4+5 sums to 12 (same total, unequal addends), a valid equal-addends discriminator.
The misconception '3+4' is handled as a clear conceptual error: the activity feedback corrects it (row-count vs row-size) rather than presenting it as a valid alternative.

Activity 3's equation-matching distractor is an unequal-addend equation (not a loosely described 'arrangement'), so the choice set stays internally consistent; its feedback draws and shades the represented ragged arrangement to show the rows are unequal.

probeDeeper: Which number in 4 + 4 + 4 is the amount in a row, and which tells how many rows?
If one row had 4 and another had 5, could you still add the same number each time?
How would you write this array as a multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — every row has the same number, 4, and there are 3 rows, so the total is 4 added three times. Equal rows let you add the row-amount repeatedly instead of counting every dot.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the dimensions, not the equal rows — writes something like 3 + 4 (row-count plus row-size) instead of repeated equal addends
errorPatterns.nextMove: shade one row (4), then show it repeats 3 times → 4 + 4 + 4; distinguish the number of rows from the amount in each row
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 + 4 works because there are 3 rows and 4 in each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an addition that isn't repeated equal addends

errorPatterns.pattern: agrees the sum but not the reason — accepts 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 yet justifies only 'because it makes 12', not because the rows are equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: cover the rows one at a time to show each contributes the same 4; name equality as what licenses repeated addition
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct sum with no equal-rows reason

errorPatterns.pattern: counts by ones only — insists you must count every dot; repeated addition feels untrustworthy
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT push the shortcut — let the child verify by counting a few times so repeated addition earns trust; the shortcut is adopted with experience
errorPatterns.revealedBy: won't accept 4 + 4 + 4 without counting to confirm

responseLevels.gap: Can only get the total by counting every object; can't connect it to repeated addition.
responseLevels.full: Explains repeated addition works because every row holds the same number, and moves between array, equal-addends sum, and multiplication.
responseLevels.partial: Writes or accepts the repeated-addition equation but doesn't ground it in the rows being equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this array — 3 rows with 4 dots in each row. Sam counted the dots one by one and got 12. Priya wrote 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 without counting them all. Is Priya's way correct, and why does adding 4 three times work for this array?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the array's equal-groups structure explains that repeated addition works BECAUSE the rows are equal. A child without it accepts 12 as 'the count' but can't say why 4 + 4 + 4 matches, or writes an addition that ignores equal rows (e.g. 3 + 4). The 'why does adding 4 three times work' tier forces the equal-addends reasoning.
